module.title: Comparative Adjectives: Comparing People & Things
module.objective: Compare two people, objects, or places accurately using regular and irregular comparative adjectives (-er than, more ... than).

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Comparing People & Things Around Us

content.summary: Welcome to your Reading Mission! In this lesson, you will read a fun passage about two friends who compare their cities, their belongings, and even their pets! You will learn how to spot comparative adjectives in a text, understand when writers use '-er than' for short adjectives and 'more ... than' for longer adjectives, and notice irregular forms like 'better than' and 'worse than'. By the end of this mission, you will feel confident reading simple English texts that compare two people, things, or places. Let's get started!

linguisticTarget.grammar: Comparative adjective patterns: short adjective + -er + than (e.g., taller than, cheaper than), more + long adjective + than (e.g., more expensive than, more comfortable than), and irregular comparatives (good → better than, bad → worse than).
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Adjectives describing size, speed, cost, comfort, weight, and quality — used in everyday comparisons between people, objects, and places.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scan the passage for comparison signal words like 'than', '-er', and 'more'. These words help you quickly find the main comparisons the writer is making. Also, skim the whole text first to understand the general topic before reading for details.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short A1 passage about comparing two cities and everyday items.
Identify key details including which things are bigger, cheaper, faster, or more comfortable.
Recognize comparative adjective patterns (-er than, more ... than, better than) used in the passage.
Distinguish between short adjective comparatives and long adjective comparatives while reading.
Build confidence reading natural English sentences that compare two people, things, or places.

contextWarmup.prompt: Read this sentence and choose the correct comparative form: 'My city is ______ your city.'
contextWarmup.explanation: 'Big' is a short adjective (one syllable), so we add -er and double the final consonant: 'bigger than'. We do NOT use 'more' with short adjectives. 'Most' is for superlatives, not comparatives. Great job if you got this right!

rules: When you see 'than' in a sentence, look at the adjective before it. This is a comparison between two things. For example: 'My bag is heavier than your bag.'
Short adjectives (one syllable like tall, fast, cheap) use the pattern: adjective + -er + than. For example: 'She is taller than her sister.'
Long adjectives (two or more syllables like expensive, comfortable, interesting) use the pattern: more + adjective + than. For example: 'This hotel is more comfortable than that one.'
Some adjectives are irregular and do not follow the -er or more rules. Remember: good → better than, bad → worse than. For example: 'This restaurant is better than the old one.'
Never mix '-er' and 'more' together. Do NOT say 'more taller' or 'more cheaper'. Choose only one form.

commonTrap.explanation: Many beginners mix up the two comparative rules. They add both 'more' and '-er' to the same adjective, or they forget to include 'than' after the comparative form. When reading, watch carefully: if you see '-er' on the adjective, there should be NO 'more' before it. And always look for 'than' to confirm it is a comparison.
commonTrap.wrong: This phone is more cheaper than that one.
commonTrap.correct: This phone is cheaper than that one.

sections.title: Reading Passage: Two Cities, Two Friends

content.context: Rina lives in Jakarta and her friend Tom lives in Yogyakarta. They are chatting online and comparing their cities, their phones, and their daily lives. Read their conversation and notice how they use comparative adjectives.
content.text:
Rina and Tom are good friends. Rina lives in Jakarta and Tom lives in Yogyakarta. They like to compare their cities.

Rina says, "Jakarta is bigger than Yogyakarta. It's also more crowded than your city. The traffic is worse than in Yogyakarta!"

Tom laughs and says, "That's true! But Yogyakarta is quieter than Jakarta. The food here is cheaper than in Jakarta too. And I think the traditional markets are more interesting than the big malls."

Rina agrees. "Yes, the markets are nice! But my new phone is faster than yours!" she jokes.

Tom replies, "Maybe, but my backpack is heavier than yours because I carry many books. I think books are better than phones for learning!"

They both laugh. Each city is different, but both are wonderful places to live.

highlights.note: Short adjective 'big' → double the final consonant + -er + than
'Crowded' has two syllables, so we use 'more ... than'
'Interesting' is a long adjective, so we use 'more ... than'
'Heavy' ends in -y, so change y to i and add -er: 'heavier than'

gistQuestion.prompt: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Two friends compare their cities, belongings, and daily lives using comparative adjectives.
Two friends are angry because their cities are very different.
Two friends want to move to a new city together.
gistQuestion.explanation: The passage is about Rina and Tom comparing Jakarta and Yogyakarta, their phones, and their habits. They use many comparative adjectives like 'bigger than', 'cheaper than', and 'better than'. They are friendly and having fun — they are not angry or planning to move!

detailQuestions.prompt: According to the passage, which city is bigger?
detailQuestions.explanation: Rina says, 'Jakarta is bigger than Yogyakarta.' This clearly tells us that Jakarta is the bigger city. Well done if you found this detail!

detailQuestions.prompt: Why is Tom's backpack heavier than Rina's?
options: Because he carries a big phone.
Because he carries food from the market.
detailQuestions.explanation: Tom says, 'My backpack is heavier than yours because I carry many books.' The reason is clearly stated in the text — he has many books in his backpack.

detailQuestions.prompt: What does Tom think is better than phones for learning?
detailQuestions.explanation: Tom says, 'I think books are better than phones for learning!' He uses the irregular comparative 'better than' (from 'good') to share his opinion about books.

detailQuestions.prompt: According to Tom, what is cheaper in Yogyakarta than in Jakarta?
detailQuestions.explanation: Tom says, 'The food here is cheaper than in Jakarta too.' He is talking about food prices in Yogyakarta compared to Jakarta.

questions.question: In the passage, Rina says the traffic in Jakarta is ______ in Yogyakarta. Which word correctly fills the blank?
questions.explanation: 'Bad' is an irregular adjective. Its comparative form is 'worse than', NOT 'badder than' or 'more bad than'. Rina says the traffic in Jakarta is worse than in Yogyakarta.

questions.question: Which sentence from the passage uses a comparative form for a LONG adjective?
options: The traditional markets are more interesting than the big malls.
My new phone is faster than yours.
The food here is cheaper than in Jakarta.
questions.answer: The traditional markets are more interesting than the big malls.
questions.explanation: 'Interesting' is a long adjective (three syllables), so it uses 'more ... than'. The other options use short adjective comparatives: 'faster' and 'cheaper' both use the -er pattern.

questions.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'Yogyakarta is quieter than Jakarta.' What does this tell us?
options: Yogyakarta has less noise than Jakarta.
Yogyakarta has more people than Jakarta.
questions.answer: Yogyakarta has less noise than Jakarta.
questions.explanation: 'Quieter' means 'more quiet' — it describes a place with less noise. If Yogyakarta is quieter than Jakarta, it means Yogyakarta has less noise. Great reading!

questions.question: How many comparative adjectives can you find in this sentence? 'Jakarta is bigger than Yogyakarta and more crowded than Yogyakarta.'
questions.explanation: There are two comparative adjectives: 'bigger than' (short adjective + -er) and 'more crowded than' (long adjective with 'more'). Each one compares Jakarta to Yogyakarta.

questions.question: At the end of the passage, what do Rina and Tom agree about?
options: Each city is different, but both are wonderful places to live.
Jakarta is better than Yogyakarta in every way.
They should stop comparing their cities.
questions.answer: Each city is different, but both are wonderful places to live.
questions.explanation: The last sentence says, 'Each city is different, but both are wonderful places to live.' Rina and Tom appreciate both cities. They do not say one city is better than the other overall.

questions.question: Which comparative form is INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: 'Cheap' is a short adjective, so the correct comparative is 'cheaper than'. You should NEVER combine 'more' and '-er' together. 'More comfortable than' and 'taller than' are both correct.

questions.question: In the passage, Tom says the traditional markets are 'more interesting than the big malls.' What is Tom comparing?
questions.explanation: Tom directly compares 'the traditional markets' with 'the big malls'. The word 'than' connects the two things being compared. He thinks markets are more interesting!

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Which Phone Is Better?

content.summary: In this listening mission, you will hear two friends comparing their smartphones at a cafe. They use comparative adjectives to talk about size, price, speed, and quality. Listen carefully for words that end in '-er than' and phrases with 'more ... than'. These are comparative forms. Short adjectives like 'big', 'cheap', and 'fast' add '-er than'. Longer adjectives like 'expensive' use 'more ... than'. Also listen for irregular comparatives like 'better than'. Pay attention to the word 'than' because it tells you a comparison is happening.
learningObjectives: Identify comparative adjective forms such as 'bigger than', 'cheaper than', and 'faster than' when spoken in natural conversation.
Recognize the phrase 'more expensive than' as a comparative form for longer adjectives.
Understand the irregular comparative 'better than' and distinguish it from 'good'.
Catch the key comparison word 'than' in connected speech, even when it is reduced to a weak sound.

keyPhrases.note: Used to compare the size of two things. 'Big' becomes 'bigger' by doubling the final consonant and adding '-er'.
Used to compare the price of two items. 'Cheap' adds '-er' to form the comparative.
Longer adjectives like 'expensive' use 'more' before the adjective instead of adding '-er'.
This is an irregular comparative. 'Good' does not become 'gooder'. It changes to 'better'.
Used to compare speed. 'Fast' simply adds '-er' to become 'faster'.
Used to compare the quality of photos or images. 'Clear' adds '-er' to form the comparative.

connectedSpeech.slow: It is bigger than my old phone.
connectedSpeech.fast: It's bigger th'n my old phone.
connectedSpeech.slowIpa: /ɪt ɪz ˈbɪɡ.ər ðæn maɪ oʊld foʊn/
connectedSpeech.note: In fast speech, 'it is' contracts to 'it's' and 'than' reduces to a weak schwa sound /ðən/. Listen for the '-er' ending to catch the comparative.

connectedSpeech.slow: Is it more expensive than mine?
connectedSpeech.fast: Is it more expensive th'n mine?
connectedSpeech.note: The word 'than' is almost always reduced in natural speech. It sounds like 'th'n' with a very short vowel. Focus on hearing 'more' before the adjective.

connectedSpeech.slow: It is faster than most phones.
connectedSpeech.note: Again, 'it is' becomes 'it's' and 'than' weakens. The stress falls on 'faster', making it the easiest word to hear in the sentence.
In fast speech, 'battery' loses its middle vowel and sounds like two syllables: 'bat-ree'. The comparative 'longer' is clearly stressed.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Comparing People & Things with Comparative Adjectives

content.summary: In this writing blueprint, you will learn how to build sentences that compare two people, things, or places. You will use comparative adjectives with 'than' to show differences. For short adjectives (one syllable), add -er than. For long adjectives (two or more syllables), use more + adjective + than. Some adjectives are irregular, like good → better than and bad → worse than. Follow the steps below to write clear comparison sentences and short paragraphs.

blueprintItems.title: Short Adjective Comparisons (-er than)
blueprintItems.example: My brother is taller than me.

blueprintItems.title: Long Adjective Comparisons (more ... than)
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + is/are + more + adjective + than + noun/pronoun.
blueprintItems.example: This restaurant is more expensive than that café.

blueprintItems.title: Irregular Adjective Comparisons
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + is/are + irregular comparative form + than + noun/pronoun.
blueprintItems.example: Her English is better than mine.

blueprintItems.title: Building a Comparison Paragraph
blueprintItems.formula: Topic sentence + 2–3 comparison sentences + closing sentence.
blueprintItems.example: My city is bigger than my friend's city. It is more crowded than her town. But her town is quieter than my city. I think both places are nice.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always use 'than' after the comparative adjective when you compare two things.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: She is taller than her sister.
mechanicsRules.why: The word 'than' connects the two things you are comparing. Without 'than', the sentence is incomplete and unclear.

mechanicsRules.rule: For short adjectives ending in a consonant-vowel-consonant pattern, double the last consonant before adding -er.
mechanicsRules.badExample: This box is biger than that one.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: This box is bigger than that one.
mechanicsRules.why: When a short adjective ends in consonant-vowel-consonant (like 'big'), you must double the final consonant: big → bigger. This is a spelling rule.

mechanicsRules.rule: Do not mix the two comparative forms. Do not say 'more taller' or 'more bigger'.
mechanicsRules.badExample: He is more taller than his friend.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: He is taller than his friend.
mechanicsRules.why: You use either -er (for short adjectives) or more (for long adjectives), but never both together. Using both is a common mistake.

mechanicsRules.rule: Start every sentence with a capital letter and end with a period, question mark, or exclamation mark.
mechanicsRules.badExample: my phone is newer than yours
mechanicsRules.goodExample: My phone is newer than yours.
mechanicsRules.why: Every English sentence must begin with a capital letter and end with proper punctuation. This makes your writing clear and correct.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Comparing People & Things with Comparative Adjectives

content.summary: In this speaking lab, you will practise saying comparative adjectives out loud. Comparative adjectives help you compare two people, things, or places. For short adjectives, we add '-er than' (bigger than, taller than). For long adjectives, we say 'more ... than' (more beautiful than, more expensive than). Good pronunciation and natural stress are very important when you speak these comparisons. Listen carefully to where the stress falls and how your voice rises or falls at the end of sentences.
content.audioGuidance: When you say comparative sentences, stress the comparative word. For example, say 'BIG-ger than' with strong stress on 'BIG'. For longer comparisons, stress the main adjective: 'more ex-PEN-sive than'. In questions like 'Which city is bigger?', your voice should rise at the end. In statements like 'Jakarta is bigger than Surabaya', your voice should fall at the end. Practise speaking slowly and clearly first, then try to speak at a natural speed.

pillars.name: Stress on Comparatives
pillars.target: Correct syllable stress on comparative adjective forms
pillars.explanation: When you say a comparative adjective, put strong stress on the main syllable. For example: 'TALL-er', 'CHEAP-er', 'more BEAU-ti-ful'. The word 'than' is usually unstressed and spoken quickly.

pillars.name: Intonation in Comparison Statements
pillars.target: Falling intonation at the end of comparative statements
pillars.explanation: When you make a statement comparing two things, your voice should go down at the end. For example: 'My house is bigger than your house.' ↘ This falling tone shows you are giving information, not asking a question.

pillars.name: Intonation in Comparison Questions
pillars.target: Rising intonation in yes/no comparison questions
pillars.explanation: When you ask a yes/no question with comparatives, your voice should go up at the end. For example: 'Is Jakarta bigger than Surabaya?' ↗ But for 'which' questions, your voice goes down: 'Which city is bigger?' ↘

pillars.name: Clear Articulation of '-er than'
pillars.target: Smooth linking of the '-er than' ending
pillars.explanation: Many learners pause too long between '-er' and 'than'. Try to link them smoothly: 'bigger-than' should sound almost like one word. The 'th' in 'than' is a soft /ð/ sound — put your tongue lightly between your teeth.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The stress stays on the first syllable 'CHEAP'. When we add '-er', the new syllable 'er' is weak and unstressed. Say 'CHEAP-er' with a strong first beat.
The stress stays on 'EA'. The word gets longer with an extra syllable, but the stress does not move. Say 'EA-si-er' keeping the first syllable strong.

For long adjectives, we add 'more' before the adjective. The word 'more' is lightly stressed, but the main stress stays on 'PEN' in 'expensive'. Say 'more ex-PEN-sive' with the strongest beat on 'PEN'.
The stress stays on 'BEAU'. We add 'more' before the adjective but do not change the stress pattern of 'beautiful'. Say 'more BEAU-ti-ful' clearly.

drills.focus: Stress on 'BIG-ger' and smooth linking with 'than'
drills.hint: Say 'BIG-ger-than' almost as one smooth phrase. Stress the 'BIG' part strongly and let 'than' be quick and soft.

drills.targetText: This book is more interesting than that book.
drills.phonetic: /ðɪs bʊk ɪz mɔːr ˈɪntrəstɪŋ ðən ðæt bʊk/
drills.focus: Stress on 'IN-ter-est-ing' and natural rhythm with 'more'
drills.hint: Put the main stress on 'IN' in 'interesting'. Say 'more' lightly before it. Let your voice fall at the end of the sentence.

drills.targetText: My sister is taller than me.
drills.focus: Clear pronunciation of 'TALL-er' and the /ð/ in 'than'
drills.hint: For the 'th' in 'than', put your tongue gently between your teeth and make a soft buzzing sound. Do not say 'dan'.
This is a 'which' question, so your voice should go DOWN at the end on 'beautiful'. Start the question with a clear 'W' sound.

drills.targetText: Is your house cheaper than this apartment?
drills.phonetic: /ɪz jɔːr haʊs ˈtʃiːpər ðən ðɪs əˈpɑːrtmənt/
drills.hint: This is a yes/no question. Your voice should go UP at the end on 'apartment'. Stress 'CHEAP-er' clearly in the middle.

drills.targetText: The weather today is hotter than yesterday.
drills.phonetic: /ðə ˈweðər təˈdeɪ ɪz ˈhɒtər ðən ˈjestərdeɪ/
drills.focus: Double consonant sound in 'hotter' and sentence rhythm
drills.hint: In 'hotter', the 't' sound is short and sharp. Say 'HOT-ter' with a quick stop on the double 't'. Your voice falls at the end.

roleplay.context: You are chatting with Mr. Khoirul about two cities: Jakarta and Surabaya. He will ask you to compare them using comparative adjectives. Try to use '-er than' for short adjectives and 'more ... than' for long adjectives. Speak clearly and use natural intonation.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Hello! Have you ever been to both Jakarta and Surabaya?
turns.translation: Halo! Apakah kamu pernah ke Jakarta dan Surabaya?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes, I have visited both cities.
turns.translation: Ya, saya sudah mengunjungi kedua kota itu.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Great! Which city do you think is bigger?
turns.translation: Bagus! Menurutmu kota mana yang lebih besar?

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: That's correct! Now, tell me about the traffic. Which city has worse traffic?
turns.translation: Benar! Sekarang, ceritakan tentang lalu lintasnya. Kota mana yang lalu lintasnya lebih buruk?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I think Jakarta has worse traffic than Surabaya.
turns.translation: Saya rasa Jakarta lalu lintasnya lebih buruk daripada Surabaya.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Good comparison! What about the food? Which city do you think has more delicious food?
turns.translation: Perbandingan yang bagus! Bagaimana dengan makanannya? Menurutmu kota mana yang makanannya lebih enak?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Both are great, but I think Surabaya has more delicious street food than Jakarta.
turns.translation: Keduanya enak, tapi saya rasa Surabaya punya jajanan kaki lima yang lebih enak daripada Jakarta.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story comparing two friends you know. Use comparative adjectives to describe how they are different. Follow the story points below and speak for about 30 seconds.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now I want you to tell me about two of your friends. Compare them using words like taller, shorter, funnier, or more serious. Follow the three points on your screen.
storyPoints: Introduce your two friends and say their names.
Compare their appearance using at least two comparative adjectives (for example: taller, shorter, older, younger).
Compare their personalities using at least one comparative adjective (for example: funnier, more serious, more friendly).
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I have two friends. Rina is taller than Sinta. Rina is also more serious than Sinta, but Sinta is funnier than Rina.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ hæv tuː frendz. ˈriːnə ɪz ˈtɔːlər ðən ˈsɪntə. ˈriːnə ɪz ˈɔːlsoʊ mɔːr ˈsɪəriəs ðən ˈsɪntə bʌt ˈsɪntə ɪz ˈfʌniər ðən ˈriːnə/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember to stress the comparative word: 'TALL-er', 'FUN-ni-er', 'more SE-ri-ous'. Let your voice fall at the end of each statement.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This storytelling task helps you practise using comparative adjectives in connected speech. When you compare two people, always use 'than' after the comparative form. Short adjectives take '-er than' and long adjectives take 'more ... than'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story comparing two places you have visited or know well. Use comparative adjectives to describe the differences. Follow the story points below.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now please tell me about two places you know. Maybe two cities, two parks, or two restaurants. Compare them using comparative adjectives. Follow the three points on your screen.
storyPoints: Name the two places and say where they are.
Compare the size or distance of the two places using comparative adjectives (for example: bigger, smaller, closer, farther).
Compare something else about the two places, like the weather, the people, or the food (for example: hotter, colder, more crowded, more peaceful).
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I know two parks. The city park is bigger than the park near my house. The city park is also more crowded than the small park, but the small park is quieter and more peaceful.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ noʊ tuː pɑːrks. ðə ˈsɪti pɑːrk ɪz ˈbɪɡər ðən ðə pɑːrk nɪər maɪ haʊs. ðə ˈsɪti pɑːrk ɪz ˈɔːlsoʊ mɔːr ˈkraʊdɪd ðən ðə smɔːl pɑːrk bʌt ðə smɔːl pɑːrk ɪz ˈkwaɪətər ænd mɔːr ˈpiːsfəl/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'than' after every comparative adjective. For short words like 'big', say 'bigger than'. For long words like 'crowded', say 'more crowded than'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Comparing places is a very common use of comparative adjectives. This task builds your confidence in using both '-er than' and 'more ... than' forms in a natural story.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are shopping with a friend. You are looking at two phones in a shop. Your friend asks you to compare them. Use comparative adjectives to answer.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Let's pretend we are in a phone shop together. I will ask you about two phones. Compare them using comparative adjectives like cheaper, better, more expensive, or more popular.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You and your friend are standing in a phone shop. There are two phones on the table: Phone A is small and cheap, and Phone B is big and expensive. Your friend wants your opinion before buying one.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are the helpful friend giving advice about which phone is better. Compare the two phones using comparative adjectives.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Phone B is bigger than Phone A, but Phone A is cheaper than Phone B.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /foʊn biː ɪz ˈbɪɡər ðən foʊn eɪ bʌt foʊn eɪ ɪz ˈtʃiːpər ðən foʊn biː/
practicumQuestions.hint: Compare the phones using simple comparative forms: 'bigger than', 'cheaper than', 'more expensive than'. Speak clearly and stress the comparative word.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Shopping is a real-life situation where you often compare things. This roleplay helps you practise using comparatives naturally in a conversation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are talking to your teacher about two students in your class. Your teacher asks you to compare them. Use comparative adjectives.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: I am your teacher. Tell me about two students in your class. Who is taller? Who is more hardworking? Compare them for me.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are in a classroom after school. Your teacher, Mr. Khoirul, wants to know more about two students: Adi and Budi. He asks you to compare their height, their study habits, and their personalities.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a student describing and comparing two classmates to your teacher. Use comparative adjectives like taller, smarter, more hardworking, and friendlier.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Adi is taller than Budi, but Budi is more hardworking than Adi.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈɑːdi ɪz ˈtɔːlər ðən ˈbuːdi bʌt ˈbuːdi ɪz mɔːr ˈhɑːrdˌwɜːrkɪŋ ðən ˈɑːdi/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use '-er than' for short adjectives like 'tall' and 'smart'. Use 'more ... than' for long adjectives like 'hardworking' and 'intelligent'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Comparing people is one of the most common uses of comparative adjectives. In this roleplay, you practise mixing short and long comparative forms in the same conversation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are at a restaurant with a friend. You have both tried two dishes. Compare the food using comparative adjectives.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: We are at a restaurant and we have tried two dishes: fried rice and noodle soup. Tell me which one you think is better and why. Use comparative adjectives.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You and your friend are sitting at a restaurant table. You have both eaten fried rice and noodle soup. Now your friend wants to know which dish you liked more and why.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a customer at a restaurant sharing your opinion about two dishes. Compare them using words like tastier, spicier, more delicious, cheaper, or bigger.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The fried rice is spicier than the noodle soup, but the noodle soup is more delicious than the fried rice.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə fraɪd raɪs ɪz ˈspaɪsiər ðən ðə ˈnuːdl suːp bʌt ðə ˈnuːdl suːp ɪz mɔːr dɪˈlɪʃəs ðən ðə fraɪd raɪs/
practicumQuestions.hint: For 'spicy', the comparative is 'spicier' (change 'y' to 'ier'). For 'delicious', use 'more delicious'. Remember to say 'than' after each comparison.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Talking about food is a fun and practical way to use comparative adjectives. This roleplay helps you compare tastes, sizes, and prices using the correct comparative forms.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are helping your younger brother choose between two schools. Compare the two schools using comparative adjectives.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Your younger brother needs to choose a school. School A is close to home and small. School B is far from home but bigger and more modern. Help him compare the two schools.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are at home with your younger brother. He has been accepted to two schools: School A (small, close, old) and School B (big, far, modern). He asks you to help him compare them so he can decide.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are the older sibling helping your brother compare two schools. Use comparative adjectives like closer, bigger, more modern, newer, and smaller.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: School A is closer than School B, but School B is bigger and more modern than School A.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /skuːl eɪ ɪz ˈkloʊsər ðən skuːl biː bʌt skuːl biː ɪz ˈbɪɡər ænd mɔːr ˈmɒdərn ðən skuːl eɪ/
practicumQuestions.hint: You can join two comparisons with 'and': 'bigger AND more modern than'. This makes your sentence sound more natural and fluent.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Making decisions often involves comparing options. This roleplay practises using comparative adjectives to give advice and express opinions about real-life choices.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following comparative adjective out loud. Make sure you pronounce the full word clearly.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say this word clearly: 'more comfortable'. This means 'lebih nyaman'. Now say the full comparison: 'This chair is more comfortable than that chair.'
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: This chair is more comfortable than that chair.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðɪs tʃeər ɪz mɔːr ˈkʌmftəbəl ðən ðæt tʃeər/
practicumQuestions.hint: The word 'comfortable' has three syllables in natural speech: 'COMF-ta-ble'. Do not say 'com-FOR-ta-ble'. Stress the first syllable.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The word 'comfortable' is often mispronounced. In natural English, it sounds like 'COMF-ter-ble' with three syllables, not four. Knowing the correct pronunciation of vocabulary is essential for clear speaking.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the grammatically correct comparative sentence out loud. Pay attention to the correct form of the comparative adjective.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Which is correct: 'She is more tall than him' or 'She is taller than him'? Say the correct sentence out loud now.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: She is taller than him.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ʃiː ɪz ˈtɔːlər ðən hɪm/
practicumQuestions.hint: 'Tall' is a short adjective with one syllable. Short adjectives use '-er than', not 'more ... than'. So we say 'taller than', not 'more tall than'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A common grammar mistake is using 'more' with short adjectives. Remember the rule: one-syllable adjectives take '-er than' (taller than, bigger than). Two-syllable adjectives ending in '-y' also take '-er than' (happier than, easier than). Longer adjectives use 'more ... than' (more beautiful than, more expensive than).

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say both words and notice how the stress changes. First say the base adjective, then say the comparative form.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen to the stress difference. Say 'ex-PEN-sive' first. Now say 'more ex-PEN-sive'. The stress stays on 'PEN' in both. Now try: 'EA-sy' and then 'EA-si-er'. The stress stays on 'EA'. Say both pairs clearly.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: This restaurant is more expensive than that restaurant. This exercise is easier than that exercise.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðɪs ˈrestərɒnt ɪz mɔːr ɪkˈspensɪv ðən ðæt ˈrestərɒnt. ðɪs ˈeksərsaɪz ɪz ˈiːziər ðən ðæt ˈeksərsaɪz/
practicumQuestions.hint: For 'expensive', the stress is always on the second syllable: 'ex-PEN-sive'. Adding 'more' does not change this. For 'easier', the stress stays on 'EA', even though the word gets longer with '-ier'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: When we change adjectives to their comparative form, the main stress usually stays on the same syllable. This is important because wrong stress can make your speech hard to understand. Practise saying the base form first, then the comparative form, and check that the stress does not move.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say both sentences and use the correct intonation pattern. The statement should have falling intonation. The question should have rising intonation.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this statement with falling intonation: 'Jakarta is bigger than Surabaya.' ↘ Your voice goes down at the end. Now say this yes/no question with rising intonation: 'Is Jakarta bigger than Surabaya?' ↗ Your voice goes up at the end. Practise both now.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Jakarta is bigger than Surabaya. Is Jakarta bigger than Surabaya?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /dʒəˈkɑːrtə ɪz ˈbɪɡər ðən ˌsʊrəˈbaɪə ↘ ɪz dʒəˈkɑːrtə ˈbɪɡər ðən ˌsʊrəˈbaɪə ↗/
practicumQuestions.hint: For statements (giving information), your voice goes DOWN at the end ↘. For yes/no questions (asking for a yes or no answer), your voice goes UP at the end ↗. The words are the same, but the music of your voice changes the meaning.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Intonation is the 'music' of English. The same words can be a statement or a question depending on whether your voice rises or falls at the end. In comparative sentences, falling intonation shows you are stating a fact. Rising intonation shows you are asking someone to confirm or deny the comparison. Mastering this difference makes your English sound much more natural.

reading.question: In the passage, Rina says the traffic in Jakarta is ______ in Yogyakarta. Which word correctly fills the blank?
reading.explanation: 'Bad' is an irregular adjective. Its comparative form is 'worse than', NOT 'badder than' or 'more bad than'. Rina says the traffic in Jakarta is worse than in Yogyakarta.

reading.question: Which sentence from the passage uses a comparative form for a LONG adjective?
options: The traditional markets are more interesting than the big malls.
My new phone is faster than yours.
The food here is cheaper than in Jakarta.
reading.answer: The traditional markets are more interesting than the big malls.
reading.explanation: 'Interesting' is a long adjective (three syllables), so it uses 'more ... than'. The other options use short adjective comparatives: 'faster' and 'cheaper' both use the -er pattern.

reading.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'Yogyakarta is quieter than Jakarta.' What does this tell us?
options: Yogyakarta has less noise than Jakarta.
Yogyakarta has more people than Jakarta.
reading.answer: Yogyakarta has less noise than Jakarta.
reading.explanation: 'Quieter' means 'more quiet' — it describes a place with less noise. If Yogyakarta is quieter than Jakarta, it means Yogyakarta has less noise. Great reading!

reading.question: How many comparative adjectives can you find in this sentence? 'Jakarta is bigger than Yogyakarta and more crowded than Yogyakarta.'
reading.explanation: There are two comparative adjectives: 'bigger than' (short adjective + -er) and 'more crowded than' (long adjective with 'more'). Each one compares Jakarta to Yogyakarta.

reading.question: At the end of the passage, what do Rina and Tom agree about?
options: Each city is different, but both are wonderful places to live.
Jakarta is better than Yogyakarta in every way.
They should stop comparing their cities.
reading.answer: Each city is different, but both are wonderful places to live.
reading.explanation: The last sentence says, 'Each city is different, but both are wonderful places to live.' Rina and Tom appreciate both cities. They do not say one city is better than the other overall.

reading.question: Which comparative form is INCORRECT?
reading.explanation: 'Cheap' is a short adjective, so the correct comparative is 'cheaper than'. You should NEVER combine 'more' and '-er' together. 'More comfortable than' and 'taller than' are both correct.

reading.question: In the passage, Tom says the traditional markets are 'more interesting than the big malls.' What is Tom comparing?
reading.explanation: Tom directly compares 'the traditional markets' with 'the big malls'. The word 'than' connects the two things being compared. He thinks markets are more interesting!

reading.question: What time does the train to London depart?
reading.explanation: Standard timetable questions provide specific morning departure times.

reading.question: Choose the correct past form: 'Yesterday, we _____ a new car.'
reading.explanation: 'Buy' is an irregular verb whose past simple form is 'bought'.

reading.question: What does Maria do every Saturday morning?
reading.explanation: A routine action in the simple present tense describing Saturday morning.

reading.question: Which question is grammatically correct?
reading.explanation: Standard question order: Question Word + Auxiliary (do) + Subject (you) + Verb (live).

reading.question: What is the opposite of 'expensive'?
reading.explanation: 'Cheap' means low in price, which is the direct opposite of 'expensive'.

reading.question: Choose the correct preposition: 'The keys are _____ the table.'
reading.explanation: We use 'on' when an object is physically resting on a surface.

reading.question: Which sentence expresses a future plan?
options: I am going to visit my grandmother tomorrow.
I visit my grandmother every day.
reading.answer: I am going to visit my grandmother tomorrow.
reading.explanation: 'Be going to' expresses a planned future intention.

reading.question: What can you buy at a pharmacy?
reading.explanation: Pharmacies specialize in dispensing medicines and healthcare supplies.

writing.prompt: Write 3 sentences comparing your phone to your friend's phone. Use at least one short adjective comparison (-er than) and one long adjective comparison (more ... than).
writing.criteria: The answer must contain 3 complete sentences. Each sentence must use a comparative adjective with 'than'. At least one sentence uses a short adjective (-er than) and at least one uses a long adjective (more ... than). All sentences must start with a capital letter and end with a period.
writing.sampleGoodAnswer: My phone is newer than my friend's phone. My friend's phone is cheaper than mine. But my phone is more expensive than his phone.

writing.prompt: Write a short paragraph (4–5 sentences) comparing two animals. For example, compare a cat and a dog, or an elephant and a mouse. Use at least one irregular comparative (better, worse, or farther).
writing.criteria: The answer must contain 4–5 sentences about two animals. It must include at least two different comparative forms and one irregular comparative. Sentences must be grammatically correct with proper capitalization and punctuation.
writing.sampleGoodAnswer: Dogs are bigger than cats. Cats are quieter than dogs. Dogs are better at playing games than cats. But cats are more independent than dogs. I think dogs are more fun than cats.

writing.prompt: Your friend asks: 'Which is better, studying at home or studying at a library?' Write 4 sentences to answer. Compare the two places using comparative adjectives.
writing.criteria: The answer must contain 4 complete sentences comparing studying at home and studying at a library. It must use at least 3 different comparative adjectives. The response must include the word 'than' in at least 3 sentences. Proper capitalization and punctuation are required.
writing.sampleGoodAnswer: A library is quieter than my home. Studying at home is more comfortable than studying at a library. But a library is better for concentration than my home. My home is closer than the library, so sometimes I study at home.

speaking.phonetic: /dʒəˈkɑːrtə ɪz ˈbɪɡər ðən ˌsʊrəˈbaɪə ↘ ɪz dʒəˈkɑːrtə ˈbɪɡər ðən ˌsʊrəˈbaɪə ↗/

speaking.explanation: Intonation is the 'music' of English. The same words can be a statement or a question depending on whether your voice rises or falls at the end. In comparative sentences, falling intonation shows you are stating a fact. Rising intonation shows you are asking someone to confirm or deny the comparison. Mastering this difference makes your English sound much more natural.

questions.instruction: Say the grammatically correct comparative sentence out loud. Pay attention to the correct form of the comparative adjective.

questions.explanation: A common grammar mistake is using 'more' with short adjectives. Remember the rule: one-syllable adjectives take '-er than' (taller than, bigger than). Two-syllable adjectives ending in '-y' also take '-er than' (happier than, easier than). Longer adjectives use 'more ... than' (more beautiful than, more expensive than).

questions.instruction: Say both words and notice how the stress changes. First say the base adjective, then say the comparative form.
questions.audioPrompt: Listen to the stress difference. Say 'ex-PEN-sive' first. Now say 'more ex-PEN-sive'. The stress stays on 'PEN' in both. Now try: 'EA-sy' and then 'EA-si-er'. The stress stays on 'EA'. Say both pairs clearly.

This is important because wrong stress can make your speech hard to understand. Practise saying the base form first, then the comparative form, and check that the stress does not move.

questions.instruction: Say both sentences and use the correct intonation pattern. The statement should have falling intonation. The question should have rising intonation.
questions.audioPrompt: Say this statement with falling intonation: 'Jakarta is bigger than Surabaya.' ↘ Your voice goes down at the end. Now say this yes/no question with rising intonation: 'Is Jakarta bigger than Surabaya?' ↗ Your voice goes up at the end. Practise both now.
questions.targetSentence: Jakarta is bigger than Surabaya. Is Jakarta bigger than Surabaya?
questions.phonetic: /dʒəˈkɑːrtə ɪz ˈbɪɡər ðən ˌsʊrəˈbaɪə ↘ ɪz dʒəˈkɑːrtə ˈbɪɡər ðən ˌsʊrəˈbaɪə ↗/
questions.hint: For statements (giving information), your voice goes DOWN at the end ↘. For yes/no questions (asking for a yes or no answer), your voice goes UP at the end ↗. The words are the same, but the music of your voice changes the meaning.
questions.explanation: Intonation is the 'music' of English. The same words can be a statement or a question depending on whether your voice rises or falls at the end. In comparative sentences, falling intonation shows you are stating a fact. Rising intonation shows you are asking someone to confirm or deny the comparison. Mastering this difference makes your English sound much more natural.

practicumQuestions.question: In the passage, Rina says the traffic in Jakarta is ______ in Yogyakarta. Which word correctly fills the blank?
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Bad' is an irregular adjective. Its comparative form is 'worse than', NOT 'badder than' or 'more bad than'. Rina says the traffic in Jakarta is worse than in Yogyakarta.

practicumQuestions.question: Which sentence from the passage uses a comparative form for a LONG adjective?
options: The traditional markets are more interesting than the big malls.

practicumQuestions.answer: The traditional markets are more interesting than the big malls.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Interesting' is a long adjective (three syllables), so it uses 'more ... than'. The other options use short adjective comparatives: 'faster' and 'cheaper' both use the -er pattern.

practicumQuestions.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'Yogyakarta is quieter than Jakarta.' What does this tell us?
options: Yogyakarta has less noise than Jakarta.

practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Quieter' means 'more quiet' — it describes a place with less noise. If Yogyakarta is quieter than Jakarta, it means Yogyakarta has less noise. Great reading!

practicumQuestions.question: How many comparative adjectives can you find in this sentence? 'Jakarta is bigger than Yogyakarta and more crowded than Yogyakarta.'
practicumQuestions.explanation: There are two comparative adjectives: 'bigger than' (short adjective + -er) and 'more crowded than' (long adjective with 'more'). Each one compares Jakarta to Yogyakarta.

practicumQuestions.question: At the end of the passage, what do Rina and Tom agree about?
options: Each city is different, but both are wonderful places to live.
Jakarta is better than Yogyakarta in every way.
They should stop comparing their cities.
practicumQuestions.answer: Each city is different, but both are wonderful places to live.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The last sentence says, 'Each city is different, but both are wonderful places to live.' Rina and Tom appreciate both cities. They do not say one city is better than the other overall.

practicumQuestions.question: Which comparative form is INCORRECT?
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Cheap' is a short adjective, so the correct comparative is 'cheaper than'. You should NEVER combine 'more' and '-er' together. 'More comfortable than' and 'taller than' are both correct.

practicumQuestions.question: In the passage, Tom says the traditional markets are 'more interesting than the big malls.' What is Tom comparing?

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are shopping with a friend. You are looking at two phones in a shop. Your friend asks you to compare them. Use comparative adjectives to answer.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Let's pretend we are in a phone shop together. I will ask you about two phones. Compare them using comparative adjectives like cheaper, better, more expensive, or more popular.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You and your friend are standing in a phone shop. There are two phones on the table: Phone A is small and cheap, and Phone B is big and expensive. Your friend wants your opinion before buying one.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are the helpful friend giving advice about which phone is better. Compare the two phones using comparative adjectives.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Phone B is bigger than Phone A, but Phone A is cheaper than Phone B.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /foʊn biː ɪz ˈbɪɡər ðən foʊn eɪ bʌt foʊn eɪ ɪz ˈtʃiːpər ðən foʊn biː/
practicumQuestions.hint: Compare the phones using simple comparative forms: 'bigger than', 'cheaper than', 'more expensive than'. Speak clearly and stress the comparative word.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Shopping is a real-life situation where you often compare things. This roleplay helps you practise using comparatives naturally in a conversation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are talking to your teacher about two students in your class. Your teacher asks you to compare them. Use comparative adjectives.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: I am your teacher. Tell me about two students in your class. Who is taller? Who is more hardworking? Compare them for me.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are in a classroom after school. Your teacher, Mr. Khoirul, wants to know more about two students: Adi and Budi. He asks you to compare their height, their study habits, and their personalities.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a student describing and comparing two classmates to your teacher. Use comparative adjectives like taller, smarter, more hardworking, and friendlier.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Adi is taller than Budi, but Budi is more hardworking than Adi.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈɑːdi ɪz ˈtɔːlər ðən ˈbuːdi bʌt ˈbuːdi ɪz mɔːr ˈhɑːrdˌwɜːrkɪŋ ðən ˈɑːdi/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use '-er than' for short adjectives like 'tall' and 'smart'. Use 'more ... than' for long adjectives like 'hardworking' and 'intelligent'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Comparing people is one of the most common uses of comparative adjectives. In this roleplay, you practise mixing short and long comparative forms in the same conversation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are at a restaurant with a friend. You have both tried two dishes. Compare the food using comparative adjectives.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: We are at a restaurant and we have tried two dishes: fried rice and noodle soup. Tell me which one you think is better and why. Use comparative adjectives.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You and your friend are sitting at a restaurant table. You have both eaten fried rice and noodle soup. Now your friend wants to know which dish you liked more and why.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a customer at a restaurant sharing your opinion about two dishes. Compare them using words like tastier, spicier, more delicious, cheaper, or bigger.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The fried rice is spicier than the noodle soup, but the noodle soup is more delicious than the fried rice.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə fraɪd raɪs ɪz ˈspaɪsiər ðən ðə ˈnuːdl suːp bʌt ðə ˈnuːdl suːp ɪz mɔːr dɪˈlɪʃəs ðən ðə fraɪd raɪs/
practicumQuestions.hint: For 'spicy', the comparative is 'spicier' (change 'y' to 'ier'). For 'delicious', use 'more delicious'. Remember to say 'than' after each comparison.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Talking about food is a fun and practical way to use comparative adjectives. This roleplay helps you compare tastes, sizes, and prices using the correct comparative forms.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are helping your younger brother choose between two schools. Compare the two schools using comparative adjectives.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Your younger brother needs to choose a school. School A is close to home and small. School B is far from home but bigger and more modern. Help him compare the two schools.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are at home with your younger brother. He has been accepted to two schools: School A (small, close, old) and School B (big, far, modern). He asks you to help him compare them so he can decide.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are the older sibling helping your brother compare two schools. Use comparative adjectives like closer, bigger, more modern, newer, and smaller.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: School A is closer than School B, but School B is bigger and more modern than School A.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /skuːl eɪ ɪz ˈkloʊsər ðən skuːl biː bʌt skuːl biː ɪz ˈbɪɡər ænd mɔːr ˈmɒdərn ðən skuːl eɪ/
practicumQuestions.hint: You can join two comparisons with 'and': 'bigger AND more modern than'. This makes your sentence sound more natural and fluent.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Making decisions often involves comparing options. This roleplay practises using comparative adjectives to give advice and express opinions about real-life choices.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following comparative adjective out loud. Make sure you pronounce the full word clearly.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say this word clearly: 'more comfortable'. This means 'lebih nyaman'. Now say the full comparison: 'This chair is more comfortable than that chair.'
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: This chair is more comfortable than that chair.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðɪs tʃeər ɪz mɔːr ˈkʌmftəbəl ðən ðæt tʃeər/
practicumQuestions.hint: The word 'comfortable' has three syllables in natural speech: 'COMF-ta-ble'. Do not say 'com-FOR-ta-ble'. Stress the first syllable.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The word 'comfortable' is often mispronounced. In natural English, it sounds like 'COMF-ter-ble' with three syllables, not four. Knowing the correct pronunciation of vocabulary is essential for clear speaking.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the grammatically correct comparative sentence out loud. Pay attention to the correct form of the comparative adjective.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Which is correct: 'She is more tall than him' or 'She is taller than him'? Say the correct sentence out loud now.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: She is taller than him.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ʃiː ɪz ˈtɔːlər ðən hɪm/
practicumQuestions.hint: 'Tall' is a short adjective with one syllable. Short adjectives use '-er than', not 'more ... than'. So we say 'taller than', not 'more tall than'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A common grammar mistake is using 'more' with short adjectives. Remember the rule: one-syllable adjectives take '-er than' (taller than, bigger than). Two-syllable adjectives ending in '-y' also take '-er than' (happier than, easier than). Longer adjectives use 'more ... than' (more beautiful than, more expensive than).

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say both words and notice how the stress changes. First say the base adjective, then say the comparative form.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen to the stress difference. Say 'ex-PEN-sive' first. Now say 'more ex-PEN-sive'. The stress stays on 'PEN' in both. Now try: 'EA-sy' and then 'EA-si-er'. The stress stays on 'EA'. Say both pairs clearly.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: This restaurant is more expensive than that restaurant. This exercise is easier than that exercise.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðɪs ˈrestərɒnt ɪz mɔːr ɪkˈspensɪv ðən ðæt ˈrestərɒnt. ðɪs ˈeksərsaɪz ɪz ˈiːziər ðən ðæt ˈeksərsaɪz/
practicumQuestions.hint: For 'expensive', the stress is always on the second syllable: 'ex-PEN-sive'. Adding 'more' does not change this. For 'easier', the stress stays on 'EA', even though the word gets longer with '-ier'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: When we change adjectives to their comparative form, the main stress usually stays on the same syllable. This is important because wrong stress can make your speech hard to understand. Practise saying the base form first, then the comparative form, and check that the stress does not move.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say both sentences and use the correct intonation pattern. The statement should have falling intonation. The question should have rising intonation.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this statement with falling intonation: 'Jakarta is bigger than Surabaya.' ↘ Your voice goes down at the end. Now say this yes/no question with rising intonation: 'Is Jakarta bigger than Surabaya?' ↗ Your voice goes up at the end. Practise both now.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Jakarta is bigger than Surabaya. Is Jakarta bigger than Surabaya?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /dʒəˈkɑːrtə ɪz ˈbɪɡər ðən ˌsʊrəˈbaɪə ↘ ɪz dʒəˈkɑːrtə ˈbɪɡər ðən ˌsʊrəˈbaɪə ↗/
practicumQuestions.hint: For statements (giving information), your voice goes DOWN at the end ↘. For yes/no questions (asking for a yes or no answer), your voice goes UP at the end ↗. The words are the same, but the music of your voice changes the meaning.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Intonation is the 'music' of English. The same words can be a statement or a question depending on whether your voice rises or falls at the end. In comparative sentences, falling intonation shows you are stating a fact. Rising intonation shows you are asking someone to confirm or deny the comparison. Mastering this difference makes your English sound much more natural.
